claim: Synaptic vesicles can be released at extremely high rates.
source: Synaptic vesicles can be released at extremely high rates, which places an extraordinary demand on the recycling machinery.
evidence: This is a general statement about synaptic vesicle release that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Docked vesicles fuse along a broad active zone in response to a single stimulus.
source: We found that docked vesicles fuse along a broad active zone in response to a single stimulus, and are replenished with a time constant of about 2 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from the study using electron microscopy after channelrhodopsin stimulation.

claim: Docked vesicles are replenished with a time constant of about 2 s.
source: We found that docked vesicles fuse along a broad active zone in response to a single stimulus, and are replenished with a time constant of about 2 s.
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data showing recovery of docked vesicles over time.

claim: Endocytosis occurs within 50 ms adjacent to the dense projection.
source: Endocytosis occurs within 50 ms adjacent to the dense projection and after 1 s adjacent to adherens junctions.
evidence: This is based on direct ultrastructural observations at different time points after stimulation.

claim: Endocytosis occurs after 1 s adjacent to adherens junctions.
source: Endocytosis occurs within 50 ms adjacent to the dense projection and after 1 s adjacent to adherens junctions.
evidence: This is based on direct ultrastructural observations at different time points after stimulation.

claim: Synaptic vesicle endocytosis may occur on a millisecond time scale following a single physiological stimulus in the intact nervous system.
source: These studies suggest that synaptic vesicle endocytosis may occur on a millisecond time scale following a single physiological stimulus in the intact nervous system and is unlikely to conform to current models of endocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations of rapid endocytosis.

claim: Synaptic vesicle endocytosis is unlikely to conform to current models of endocytosis.
source: These studies suggest that synaptic vesicle endocytosis may occur on a millisecond time scale following a single physiological stimulus in the intact nervous system and is unlikely to conform to current models of endocytosis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed rapid kinetics that differ from established clathrin-mediated and kiss-and-run models.

claim: Synaptic transmission is quantal—postsynaptic responses have a uniform minimal size.
source: Synaptic transmission is quantal—postsynaptic responses have a uniform minimal size (Fatt and Katz, 1952).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the foundational work of Fatt and Katz.

claim: Fusion of synaptic vesicles with the plasma membrane accounts for the release of fixed amounts of neurotransmitter.
source: Katz hypothesized that fusion of synaptic vesicles with the plasma membrane accounted for the release of fixed amounts of neurotransmitter (Del Castillo and Katz, 1956).
evidence: This is a historical hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: After prolonged stimulation, synaptic vesicles were depleted from the terminals.
source: After prolonged stimulation, it was noted that synaptic vesicles were depleted from the terminals, suggesting that vesicles were being consumed during synaptic transmission (Ceccarelli et al., 1972, 1973; Heuser and Reese, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous ultrastructural studies.

claim: Vesicles could be observed fusing to the plasma membrane after single stimulus if synapses were rapidly frozen.
source: Later it was found by Heuser and Reese that if the synapses were rapidly frozen after single stimulus that vesicles could be observed fusing to the plasma membrane (Heuser and Reese, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the work of Heuser and Reese.

claim: The timing of vesicle fusion coincided precisely with that of transmitter release.
source: Furthermore, Torri-Tarelli et al. demonstrated that the timing of vesicle fusion coincided precisely with that of transmitter release (Torri-Tarelli et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the work of Torri-Tarelli et al.

claim: Recycling was originally inferred from standard fixations based on the presence of coated vesicles on the plasma membrane.
source: Recycling was originally inferred from standard fixations based on the presence of coated vesicles on the plasma membrane (Heuser and Reese, 1973) and the uptake of peroxidase after stimulation (Ceccarelli et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies.

claim: Invaginations were most abundant 30 s after stimulation.
source: Invaginations were most abundant 30 s after stimulation and were observed in membrane domains lateral to the active zone in freeze fracture studies (Miller and Heuser, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the work of Miller and Heuser.

claim: Recycling of synaptic vesicles was proposed to be mediated via clathrin coats.
source: Based on the presence of coated pits in traditional fixations (Heuser and Reese, 1973), it was proposed that recycling of synaptic vesicles was mediated via clathrin coats.
evidence: This is a historical proposal supported by citation.

claim: Clathrin and its adaptors are sufficient to stimulate budding from brain-derived membranes.
source: Reconstitution experiments demonstrate that clathrin and its adaptors are sufficient to stimulate budding from brain-derived membranes (Takei et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to reconstitution experiments.

claim: Synaptic vesicle proteins are found in clathrin-coated vesicles.
source: Purification of vesicles from brain demonstrated that synaptic vesicle proteins (and not just membrane) are found in clathrin-coated vesicles (Maycox et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to purification studies.

claim: Clathrin-coated pits accumulate at terminals in which vesicle scission is blocked by interfering with dynamin.
source: Furthermore, clathrin-coated pits accumulate at terminals in which vesicle scission is blocked by interfering with dynamin (Koenig and Ikeda, 1989; Shupliakov et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using dynamin mutants.

claim: Disruption of clathrin function slows the rate of endocytosis.
source: Disruption of clathrin function by peptide injections, siRNA application, or photoinactivation all slow the rate of endocytosis (Jockusch et al., 2005; Granseth et al., 2006; Heerssen et al., 2008; Kasprowicz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple functional studies.

claim: Synaptic vesicle proteins tagged with pHlourin are recycled in about 15 s.
source: Finally, synaptic vesicle proteins tagged with pHlourin are recycled in about 15 s, roughly the same speed as membrane recycling observed in ultrastructural experiments (Granseth et al., 2006; Balaji and Ryan, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to optical imaging studies.

claim: During locomotion, lumbar motor neurons in the mouse can fire at ∼100 Hz.
source: For example, during locomotion, lumbar motor neurons in the mouse can fire at ∼100 Hz (Maeno-Hikichi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to physiological measurements.

claim: In the Calyx of Held, firing rates can reach up to 500 Hz.
source: Moreover, in some central synapses such as the Calyx of Held, firing rates can reach up to 500 Hz (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2008; Lorteije et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: Vesicles are reused every 13 s at the Calyx of Held.
source: Calculations suggest that vesicles are reused every 13 s at the Calyx of Held, assuming that all the vesicles in the terminal are mobile (Neher, 2010).
evidence: This is based on calculations cited from Neher's work.

claim: Only 5–20% of vesicles in the terminal are cycling during physiological activity.
source: Furthermore, experiments using FM dyes suggest that only 5–20% of vesicles in the terminal are cycling during physiological activity (Harata et al., 2001; Rizzoli and Betz, 2005; Denker et al., 2011; Marra et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to FM dye studies.

claim: Vesicles with fusion pores lacking clathrin coats were observed in the active zone when frog neuromuscular junctions were stimulated at low frequency.
source: When frog neuromuscular junctions were stimulated at low frequency, vesicles with fusion pores lacking clathrin coats were observed in the active zone (Ceccarelli et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ceccarelli's observations.

claim: The fusion pores are unstable, lasting about a second.
source: The fusion pores are unstable, lasting about a second (Wu and Wu, 2009; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies measuring fusion pore dynamics.

claim: Some experiments using optical tracers support a fast pathway for endocytosis.
source: Some experiments using optical tracers including FM dyes, pH-sensitive fluorescent proteins, and quantum dots support a fast pathway (Richards et al., 2000, 2005; Aravanis et al., 2003; Harata et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007, 2009; Zhu et al., 2009; Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple optical imaging studies.

claim: Under high-frequency stimulation bulk endocytosis contributes to vesicle recycling.
source: Under high-frequency stimulation bulk endocytosis contributes to vesicle recycling (Smith et al., 2008; Cousin, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of bulk endocytosis.

claim: Bulk endocytosis has been observed following intense stimulation at frog neuromuscular junctions.
source: Bulk endocytosis has been observed following intense stimulation at frog neuromuscular junctions (Miller and Heuser, 1984; Richards et al., 2000; Gaffield et al., 2011), retinal bipolar cells (Holt et al., 2003), and mammalian central synapses (Clayton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies across different preparations.

claim: High-pressure freezing can freeze a sample as thick as 200 µm within 25 ms with reduced ice crystal formation.
source: We employed high-pressure freezing because it can freeze a sample as thick as 200 µm within 25 ms with reduced ice crystal formation (Moor and Riehle, 1968; Moor, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the technical literature on high-pressure freezing.

claim: Channelrhodopsin-2 can be expressed in C. elegans motor neurons to stimulate neurotransmission with pulses of light.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that channelrhodopsin-2 (Nagel et al., 2003) can be expressed in Caenorhabditis elegans motor neurons to stimulate neurotransmission with pulses of light (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The amplitudes of evoked responses triggered by ChIEF are similar to electrically stimulated responses.
source: The amplitudes of evoked responses triggered by ChIEF are similar to electrically stimulated responses, suggesting that ChIEF activation can cause the simultaneous fusion of about 100 synaptic vesicles per muscle cell or approximately 4–10 synaptic vesicles per synapse.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing ChIEF and electrical stimulation.

claim: ChIEF activation can cause the simultaneous fusion of about 100 synaptic vesicles per muscle cell.
source: The amplitudes of evoked responses triggered by ChIEF are similar to electrically stimulated responses, suggesting that ChIEF activation can cause the simultaneous fusion of about 100 synaptic vesicles per muscle cell or approximately 4–10 synaptic vesicles per synapse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the amplitude of postsynaptic currents.

claim: ChIEF activation causes approximately 4–10 synaptic vesicles to fuse per synapse.
source: The amplitudes of evoked responses triggered by ChIEF are similar to electrically stimulated responses, suggesting that ChIEF activation can cause the simultaneous fusion of about 100 synaptic vesicles per muscle cell or approximately 4–10 synaptic vesicles per synapse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the amplitude of postsynaptic currents and the number of synapses.

claim: The minimal interval between stimulation and freezing was ∼20 ms due to the mechanics of the freezing device.
source: The minimal interval between stimulation and freezing was ∼20 ms due to the mechanics of the freezing device ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a technical limitation of the experimental apparatus.

claim: Vesicles are morphologically docked along a broad stretch of the plasma membrane juxtaposed to the muscle.
source: Vesicles are morphologically docked along a broad stretch of the plasma membrane juxtaposed to the muscle and are considered to comprise the readily releasable pool (Hammarlund et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations and citation to previous work.

claim: Vesicles fusing 20 ms after stimulation have a diameter of 28.4 nm ± 0.3, the same size as a synaptic vesicle.
source: We froze animals 20 ms after stimulation and observed vesicles fusing along the plasma membrane (Figure 2A–E); the diameter of these vesicles was 28.4 nm ± 0.3, the same size as a synaptic vesicle.
evidence: This is based on direct measurements from electron micrographs.

claim: Exocytic pits were not observed in the non-stimulated control.
source: These exocytic pits were not observed in the non-stimulated control and at 30 ms after stimulation after postsynaptic currents have ended (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparison between stimulated and control conditions.

claim: The exocytic intermediates have wide openings at their necks, suggesting that vesicles fully collapse into the membrane.
source: The exocytic intermediates have wide openings at their necks, suggesting that vesicles fully collapse into the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphology of fusion intermediates observed in electron micrographs.

claim: The number of docked vesicles was reduced after the stimulus.
source: The number of docked vesicles was reduced after the stimulus (Figure 2G,H), whereas the number of tethered vesicles remained the same (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electron micrographs.

claim: The number of tethered vesicles remained the same after the stimulus.
source: The number of docked vesicles was reduced after the stimulus (Figure 2G,H), whereas the number of tethered vesicles remained the same (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electron micrographs.

claim: Docked, but not tethered, vesicles fuse in response to depolarization and thus constitute the readily releasable pool.
source: These data suggest that docked, but not tethered, vesicles fuse in response to depolarization and thus constitute the readily releasable pool (Zenisek et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective depletion of docked vesicles after stimulation.

claim: Fusing vesicles were found along the entire face of the synapse between the dense projection and the flanking cell junctions.
source: Fusing vesicles were found along the entire face of the synapse between the dense projection and the flanking cell junctions; thus the active zone for the C. elegans neuromuscular junction is rather broad (Figure 2A–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on spatial analysis of fusion events in reconstructed synapses.

claim: The active zone for the C. elegans neuromuscular junction is rather broad.
source: Fusing vesicles were found along the entire face of the synapse between the dense projection and the flanking cell junctions; thus the active zone for the C. elegans neuromuscular junction is rather broad (Figure 2A–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of fusion events.

claim: Approximately one fusion intermediate was observed per synaptic profile.
source: We quantified these events per synaptic profile, that is, in cross-sections of a synapse that contained a portion of the dense projection. On average, approximately one fusion intermediate was observed per synaptic profile although this number could be an underestimate given that neurotransmission is declining at this time point (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electron micrographs.

claim: Fusion intermediates were no longer observed 50 ms after stimulation.
source: Fusion intermediates were no longer observed 50 ms after stimulation; however, docked vesicles were depleted from the terminals (Figure 3; more micrographs in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electron micrographs at the 50 ms time point.

claim: Docked vesicles were depleted from the terminals 50 ms after stimulation.
source: Fusion intermediates were no longer observed 50 ms after stimulation; however, docked vesicles were depleted from the terminals (Figure 3; more micrographs in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electron micrographs.

claim: Fusing vesicles had collapsed into the membrane by 50 ms but release sites had not been refilled.
source: These results suggest that fusing vesicles had collapsed into the membrane by 50 ms but that release sites had not been refilled.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of fusion intermediates and continued depletion of docked vesicles.

claim: In unstimulated neurons, there were about 11 docked vesicles in the active zone lateral to the dense projection.
source: In unstimulated neurons, there were about 11 docked vesicles in the active zone lateral to the dense projection.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of unstimulated control synapses.

claim: A single stimulus caused the release of about six to seven vesicles from profiles containing a dense projection.
source: A single stimulus caused the release of about six to seven vesicles from profiles containing a dense projection, or about one third of the docked vesicles in these sections.
evidence: This is calculated from the difference in docked vesicles before and after stimulation.

claim: A single neuromuscular junction may release up to 12–18 vesicles per stimulus.
source: Thus, a single neuromuscular junction may release up to 12–18 vesicles per stimulus, in agreement with our reconstructed synapse 20 ms after stimulation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an extrapolation based on partial reconstructions and full synapse reconstructions.

claim: Docked vesicles in the perisynaptic zone were not released by a stimulus.
source: Some vesicles are docked in the perisynaptic zone beyond the adherens junctions at the far edge of the synapse, sometimes called 'ectopic docking' (Zenisek et al., 2000; Lenzi et al., 2002; Matsui and Jahr, 2003; Hammarlund et al., 2007). These perisynaptic vesicles are not released after a stimulus (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis showing no change in perisynaptic docked vesicles after stimulation.

claim: The active zone extends on either side of the dense projection to the flanking cell-cell junctions.
source: Together, these results suggest that the active zone extends on either side of the dense projection to the flanking cell-cell junctions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of vesicle depletion after stimulation.

claim: Acetylcholine neuromuscular junctions in C. elegans exhibit rapid depression when stimulated at high frequency.
source: Acetylcholine neuromuscular junctions in C. elegans exhibit rapid depression when stimulated at high frequency (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The time constant (τ) for the slow phase of recovery was 2.2 s.
source: The time constant (τ) for the slow phase of recovery was 2.2 s, and required about 6 s for full recovery (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on paired-pulse electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Full recovery from synaptic depression required about 6 s.
source: The time constant (τ) for the slow phase of recovery was 2.2 s, and required about 6 s for full recovery (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on paired-pulse electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Docked vesicles in active zones recovered with a time constant of 2.4 s.
source: Docked vesicles in active zones recovered with a time constant of 2.4 s (Figure 4C), which corresponds well to the rate of electrophysiological recovery.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of docked vesicles at different time points after stimulation.

claim: The recovery time constant for docked vesicles corresponds well to the rate of electrophysiological recovery.
source: Docked vesicles in active zones recovered with a time constant of 2.4 s (Figure 4C), which corresponds well to the rate of electrophysiological recovery.
evidence: This is a comparison between morphological and electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The total number of vesicles decreased slightly after stimulation but recovered by 300 ms.
source: The total number of vesicles, as well as tethered vesicles, decreased slightly after stimulation but recovered by 300 ms (Figure 4E,F) and can be accounted for by the number of vesicles lost through fusion.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of total vesicle numbers over time.

claim: The docked vesicles are likely the morphological correlate of the readily releasable pool.
source: Together, these results suggest that the docked vesicles are likely the morphological correlate of the readily releasable pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between morphological and electrophysiological recovery rates.

claim: About 50% of the synapses exhibited large invaginations next to the dense projection at 20 ms after stimulation.
source: At 20 ms after stimulation, about 50% of the synapses exhibited large invaginations next to the dense projection (Figure 5B,D,G and H, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of electron micrographs.

claim: Large invaginations were present 30 ms after stimulation but were completely absent by 50 ms.
source: These invaginations were present 30 ms after stimulation but were completely absent by 50 ms.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of endocytic structures.

claim: Large vesicles were adjacent to the dense projection in 50% of the synapses at 20 ms.
source: Large vesicles were adjacent to the dense projection in 50% of the synapses at 20 ms, their frequency increases at 30 ms, and peaks at 50 ms (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of large vesicles over time.

claim: The frequency of large vesicles adjacent to the dense projection peaks at 50 ms.
source: Large vesicles were adjacent to the dense projection in 50% of the synapses at 20 ms, their frequency increases at 30 ms, and peaks at 50 ms (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of large vesicles over time.

claim: Large vesicles appeared only after stimulation.
source: These large vesicles appeared only after stimulation (Figure 5B), suggesting that the formation of large vesicles is triggered by exocytosis.
evidence: This is based on comparison between stimulated and unstimulated conditions.

claim: The formation of large vesicles is triggered by exocytosis.
source: These large vesicles appeared only after stimulation (Figure 5B), suggesting that the formation of large vesicles is triggered by exocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between stimulation and large vesicle appearance.

claim: The average diameter of the large invaginations and vesicles near dense projection (42.8 nm) was significantly larger than synaptic vesicles (29.3 nm).
source: The average diameter of the large invaginations and vesicles near dense projection (42.8 nm) was significantly larger than synaptic vesicles (29.3 nm; p<0.0001) or fusing vesicles (28.4 nm; p<0.0001; Figure 5A) and the diameter was bimodally distributed (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements from electron micrographs with statistical analysis.

claim: The diameter of large vesicles near the dense projection was bimodally distributed.
source: The average diameter of the large invaginations and vesicles near dense projection (42.8 nm) was significantly larger than synaptic vesicles (29.3 nm; p<0.0001) or fusing vesicles (28.4 nm; p<0.0001; Figure 5A) and the diameter was bimodally distributed (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of size distributions.

claim: Large vesicles at the dense projection declined after 50 ms.
source: Large vesicles at the dense projection declined after 50 ms, and large vesicles peaked in the center of the synaptic varicosity between 100 ms and 300 ms.
evidence: This is based on temporal and spatial analysis of large vesicles.

claim: Large vesicles peaked in the center of the synaptic varicosity between 100 ms and 300 ms.
source: Large vesicles at the dense projection declined after 50 ms, and large vesicles peaked in the center of the synaptic varicosity between 100 ms and 300 ms.
evidence: This is based on temporal and spatial analysis of large vesicles.

claim: Large vesicles in the center of the synapse declined to background levels by 3 s suggesting that they are resolved into smaller vesicles.
source: The large vesicles in the center of the synapse declined to background levels by 3 s suggesting that they are resolved into smaller vesicles, potentially synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of large vesicle disappearance.

claim: Large vesicles do not appear after stimulation in unc-13 mutants.
source: There was no increase in the number of large vesicles next to the dense projection after stimulation (Figure 5C), although occasionally a large vesicle was observed in unstimulated unc-13 mutants.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of unc-13 mutants after stimulation.

claim: The formation of large vesicles at the dense projection requires exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
source: Thus, the formation of large vesicles at the dense projection requires exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of large vesicles in unc-13 mutants which lack exocytosis.

claim: Invaginations appeared at the flanking adherens junctions after about 100 ms.
source: After about 100 ms, invaginations appeared at the flanking adherens junctions (Figure 6A,E, and G; more example micrographs in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of endocytic structures at adherens junctions.

claim: Deep invaginations and large vesicles were observed at adherens junctions at later time points.
source: At later time points, deeper invaginations and large vesicles (Figure 6B,C; more example micrographs in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–F) were observed at adherens junctions.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of endocytic structures.

claim: The invaginations at adherens junctions appeared to lack clathrin coats.
source: These invaginations appeared to lack clathrin coats, although clathrin-coated vesicles can be observed using this sample preparation (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on morphological examination of the invaginations.

claim: The mean diameter of deep pits and large vesicles at adherens junctions was 44 nm, the equivalent of 2.3 synaptic vesicles.
source: The mean diameter of deep pits, as well as large vesicles, was 44 nm, the equivalent of 2.3 synaptic vesicles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements from electron micrographs.

claim: The prevalence of pits at adherens junctions peaks at 300 ms.
source: The prevalence of pits peaks at 300 ms (Figure 6E) and decays with a time constant of 1.4 s (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of pit numbers.

claim: Pits at adherens junctions decay with a time constant of 1.4 s.
source: The prevalence of pits peaks at 300 ms (Figure 6E) and decays with a time constant of 1.4 s (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of pit numbers.

claim: Large vesicles associated with the adherens junction peak at 3 s.
source: Large vesicles associated with the adherens junction (within 50 nm) peak at 3 s and decline, suggesting that pits are precursors to large vesicles.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of large vesicle numbers.

claim: Pits are precursors to large vesicles at adherens junctions.
source: Large vesicles associated with the adherens junction (within 50 nm) peak at 3 s and decline, suggesting that pits are precursors to large vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of pits and large vesicles.

claim: After 10 s, the number of large vesicles adjacent to the adherens junction declines to background levels, and vesicles in the center of the terminal peak at this time.
source: After 10 s, the number of large vesicles adjacent to the adherens junction declines to background levels, and vesicles in the center of the terminal peak at this time (dashed line in Figure 6E), suggesting that the vesicles were transported to the center of the terminal.
evidence: This is based on spatial and temporal analysis of vesicle distributions.

claim: Vesicles were transported from adherens junctions to the center of the terminal.
source: After 10 s, the number of large vesicles adjacent to the adherens junction declines to background levels, and vesicles in the center of the terminal peak at this time (dashed line in Figure 6E), suggesting that the vesicles were transported to the center of the terminal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial redistribution of vesicles over time.

claim: Endocytic pits did not appear in animals lacking trans-retinal.
source: Endocytic pits did not appear in animals lacking trans-retinal or in unc-13(s69) mutants (Figure 6E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), thus the formation of pits was triggered by the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is based on comparison between conditions with and without functional channelrhodopsin.

claim: Endocytic pits did not appear in unc-13(s69) mutants.
source: Endocytic pits did not appear in animals lacking trans-retinal or in unc-13(s69) mutants (Figure 6E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), thus the formation of pits was triggered by the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is based on analysis of unc-13 mutants which lack exocytosis.

claim: The formation of pits at adherens junctions was triggered by the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
source: Endocytic pits did not appear in animals lacking trans-retinal or in unc-13(s69) mutants (Figure 6E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), thus the formation of pits was triggered by the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of pits in conditions without exocytosis.

claim: A second endocytosis pathway takes place at adherens junctions.
source: Together, these results suggest that a second endocytosis pathway takes place at adherens junctions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distinct spatial and temporal characteristics of endocytosis at adherens junctions.

claim: At 300 ms after stimulation, a total of 132–154 synaptic vesicles fused to the plasma membrane for all 22 synapses analyzed.
source: We estimate that a total of 132–154 synaptic vesicles fused to the plasma membrane for all 22 synapses analyzed at the 300 ms time point and a total of 111 synaptic vesicle equivalents were recycled.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the number of docked vesicles lost per synapse.

claim: At 300 ms after stimulation, a total of 111 synaptic vesicle equivalents were recycled.
source: We estimate that a total of 132–154 synaptic vesicles fused to the plasma membrane for all 22 synapses analyzed at the 300 ms time point and a total of 111 synaptic vesicle equivalents were recycled.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the membrane area of endocytic structures.

claim: At 1 s after stimulation, a total of 138–161 synaptic vesicles were estimated to exocytose.
source: For the 1 s time point, a total of 138–161 synaptic vesicles were estimated to exocytose, and membrane area equivalent to roughly 144 synaptic vesicles was recovered.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the number of docked vesicles lost per synapse.

claim: At 1 s after stimulation, membrane area equivalent to roughly 144 synaptic vesicles was recovered.
source: For the 1 s time point, a total of 138–161 synaptic vesicles were estimated to exocytose, and membrane area equivalent to roughly 144 synaptic vesicles was recovered.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the membrane area of endocytic structures.

claim: Most vesicles that fuse during exocytosis are retrieved rapidly after exocytosis.
source: These data suggest that most vesicles that fuse during exocytosis are retrieved rapidly after exocytosis; 43% are recovered at dense projections with a time constant of less than 50 ms and 57% are recovered at adherens junctions with a time constant for pit resolution of 1.4 s (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the membrane balance calculations.

claim: 43% of vesicles are recovered at dense projections with a time constant of less than 50 ms.
source: These data suggest that most vesicles that fuse during exocytosis are retrieved rapidly after exocytosis; 43% are recovered at dense projections with a time constant of less than 50 ms and 57% are recovered at adherens junctions with a time constant for pit resolution of 1.4 s (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is calculated from the proportion of endocytic structures at each site.

claim: 57% of vesicles are recovered at adherens junctions with a time constant for pit resolution of 1.4 s.
source: These data suggest that most vesicles that fuse during exocytosis are retrieved rapidly after exocytosis; 43% are recovered at dense projections with a time constant of less than 50 ms and 57% are recovered at adherens junctions with a time constant for pit resolution of 1.4 s (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is calculated from the proportion of endocytic structures at each site and the decay kinetics.

claim: Heuser and Reese stimulated neuromuscular junctions at 10 Hz for 1 min.
source: For example, for cross sections of the frog neuromuscular junction, Heuser and Reese applied stimulation at 10 Hz for 1 min (1973), and Ceccarelli employed 2 Hz stimulation for 2 hr (1972).
evidence: This is a description of methods from cited historical studies.

claim: Ceccarelli employed 2 Hz stimulation for 2 hr.
source: For example, for cross sections of the frog neuromuscular junction, Heuser and Reese applied stimulation at 10 Hz for 1 min (1973), and Ceccarelli employed 2 Hz stimulation for 2 hr (1972).
evidence: This is a description of methods from cited historical studies.

claim: Endocytosis at the dense projection occurs very rapidly: invaginations appear at 20 ms after the stimulation and these pits have resolved into large vesicles in less than 50 ms.
source: Endocytosis at the dense projection occurs very rapidly: invaginations appear at 20 ms after the stimulation and these pits have resolved into large vesicles in less than 50 ms.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of endocytic structures at the dense projection.

claim: This rate is extremely fast compared to measures of kiss-and-run endocytosis (∼1 s) and clathrin-mediated endocytosis (15–20 s).
source: This rate is extremely fast compared to measures of kiss-and-run endocytosis (∼1 s; Zhang et al., 2009) and clathrin-mediated endocytosis (15–20 s [Miller and Heuser, 1984; Jockusch et al., 2005; Balaji and Ryan, 2007]) and we call this 'ultrafast endocytosis' to distinguish it from other models.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature values for other endocytosis mechanisms.

claim: The authors call the rapid endocytosis observed 'ultrafast endocytosis' to distinguish it from other models.
source: This rate is extremely fast compared to measures of kiss-and-run endocytosis (∼1 s; Zhang et al., 2009) and clathrin-mediated endocytosis (15–20 s [Miller and Heuser, 1984; Jockusch et al., 2005; Balaji and Ryan, 2007]) and we call this 'ultrafast endocytosis' to distinguish it from other models.
evidence: This is a definitional statement by the authors.

claim: At the adherens junction endocytosis is not as fast as at the dense projection but is still very fast.
source: At the adherens junction endocytosis is not as fast as at the dense projection but is still very fast.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the measured kinetics at both sites.

claim: Shallow pits at adherens junctions peak at 300 ms and are mostly resolved by 3 s.
source: Shallow pits peak at 300 ms and are mostly resolved by 3 s.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of pit numbers at adherens junctions.

claim: The time constant for clathrin-mediated endocytosis is reported to be ∼15–20 s.
source: The time constant for clathrin-mediated endocytosis is reported to be ∼15–20 s (Miller and Heuser, 1984; Granseth et al., 2006; Balaji and Ryan, 2007), which is in the range of the events we observe adjacent to the adherens junction.
evidence: This is based on citations to the literature.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis at synapses may be accelerated, possibly due to pre-formed clathrin cages at endocytic sites.
source: It is possible that clathrin-mediated endocytosis at synapses is accelerated, possibly due to pre-formed clathrin cages at endocytic sites (Wienisch and Klingauf, 2006), or that clathrin is not involved in these fast forms of endocytosis.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: Clathrin may not be involved in these fast forms of endocytosis.
source: It is possible that clathrin-mediated endocytosis at synapses is accelerated, possibly due to pre-formed clathrin cages at endocytic sites (Wienisch and Klingauf, 2006), or that clathrin is not involved in these fast forms of endocytosis.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Coats are preserved when neurons are fixed with glutaraldehyde.
source: Coats are preserved when neurons are fixed with glutaraldehyde (Heuser and Reese, 1973; Koenig and Ikeda, 1989; Takei et al., 1998), and coated vesicles are preserved in the conditions used here.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and the authors' own observations.

claim: Coated vesicles are preserved in the conditions used in this study.
source: Coats are preserved when neurons are fixed with glutaraldehyde (Heuser and Reese, 1973; Koenig and Ikeda, 1989; Takei et al., 1998), and coated vesicles are preserved in the conditions used here.
evidence: This is based on the authors' observations of clathrin-coated vesicles in their preparations.

claim: The absence of coats on endocytic pits is consistent with the absence of a genetic requirement for clathrin heavy chain at C. elegans neuromuscular junctions.
source: The absence of coats on endocytic pits is consistent with the absence of a genetic requirement for clathrin heavy chain at C. elegans neuromuscular junctions (Sato et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference connecting morphological observations with genetic data from the literature.

claim: Synaptic vesicles are smaller in the temperature-sensitive allele of clathrin in C. elegans.
source: In fact, synaptic vesicles are smaller in the temperature-sensitive allele of clathrin in C. elegans (Sato et al., 2009), suggesting that vesicles may pass through a clathrin-coated intermediate at the neuromuscular junction, perhaps during the resolution of endosomes.
evidence: This is based on citation to genetic studies.

claim: Vesicles may pass through a clathrin-coated intermediate at the neuromuscular junction, perhaps during the resolution of endosomes.
source: In fact, synaptic vesicles are smaller in the temperature-sensitive allele of clathrin in C. elegans (Sato et al., 2009), suggesting that vesicles may pass through a clathrin-coated intermediate at the neuromuscular junction, perhaps during the resolution of endosomes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the genetic data.

claim: Kiss-and-run endocytosis is thought to occur within about 1 s of stimulation.
source: Kiss-and-run endocytosis is thought to occur within about 1 s of stimulation (Miller and Heuser, 1984; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on citations to the literature on kiss-and-run.

claim: The appearance of endocytic structures within 50 ms after stimulation at the C. elegans neuromuscular junction is consistent with kiss-and-run endocytosis.
source: The appearance of endocytic structures within 50 ms after stimulation at the C. elegans neuromuscular junction is consistent with kiss-and-run endocytosis.
evidence: This is a comparison of the observed kinetics with the kiss-and-run model.

claim: All exocytic intermediates captured at 20 ms after stimulation at the C. elegans neuromuscular junction have wide necks, suggesting that synaptic vesicles are collapsing into the membrane.
source: All exocytic intermediates captured at 20 ms after stimulation at the C. elegans neuromuscular junction have wide necks, suggesting that synaptic vesicles are collapsing into the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphology of fusion intermediates.

claim: Vesicles fuse throughout the active zone, but endocytosis takes place at the edges of the active zone.
source: Moreover, vesicles fuse throughout the active zone, but endocytosis takes place at the edges of the active zone.
evidence: This is based on spatial analysis of fusion and endocytosis sites.

claim: A large amount of membrane must translocate to endocytic sites at the lateral margins of the synaptic membrane.
source: Although we cannot exclude the reversal of the fusion pore by some vesicles, a large amount of membrane must translocate to endocytic sites at the lateral margins of the synaptic membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial separation of fusion and endocytosis sites.

claim: The kiss-and-run model predicts that synaptic vesicles retain their integrity.
source: The kiss-and-run model predicts that synaptic vesicles retain their integrity, that is, the vesicle is recovered intact (Murthy and Stevens, 1998).
evidence: This is a description of the kiss-and-run model from the literature.

claim: Some endocytic structures adjacent to the dense projection are greater than twice the size of a synaptic vesicle.
source: However, some endocytic structures adjacent to the dense projection are greater than twice the size of a synaptic vesicle.
evidence: This is based on size measurements from electron micrographs.

claim: The arrested endocytic structures in the dynamin mutants became even larger with prolonged synaptic activity.
source: Moreover, the arrested endocytic structures in the dynamin mutants became even larger with prolonged synaptic activity.
evidence: This is based on observations in dynamin mutants.

claim: Very large trapped pits in dynamin mutants suggest that vesicles collapse into the plasma membrane and are retrieved via an endocytic pit.
source: These very large trapped pits in dynamin mutants suggest that vesicles collapse into the plasma membrane and are retrieved via an endocytic pit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the size and behavior of structures in dynamin mutants.

claim: Ultrafast endocytosis might require optogenetic stimulation methods to be observed.
source: Ultrafast endocytosis might require optogenetic stimulation methods to be observed: endocytosis is assayed in this preparation in an undissected animal.
evidence: This is speculation about why ultrafast endocytosis was observed in this study.

claim: In intact nervous systems spatial constraints may accelerate synaptic vesicle endocytosis even during low frequency activity.
source: Neurons in intact nervous systems are bundled together, thus, in intact nervous systems spatial constraints may accelerate synaptic vesicle endocytosis even during low frequency activity.
evidence: This is speculation about mechanisms that might explain the rapid endocytosis observed.

claim: Large vesicles with a diameter of 59.0 ± 5.9 nm were observed in dynamin mutants at the restrictive temperature without stimulation.
source: Following the exposure to non-permissive temperature (30°C) for 2 min, large vesicles were observed adjacent to the dense projection and adherens junctions in the non-stimulated control (Figure 7A–C; more example micrographs Figure 7—figure supplement 1). These vesicles were often associated with a filament to the dense projection or membrane. Although necks were difficult to discern, prolonged incubation at the restrictive temperature (5 min) revealed the presence of membrane necks attached to the plasma membrane (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C). Typically, 2.7 ± 0.4 large vesicles were observed in each synapse (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on observations in dynamin mutants at the restrictive temperature.

claim: Stimulation in dynamin mutants did not increase the number of large vesicles but the diameter of these structures became 1.5 times larger (from 59.0 ± 5.9 nm to 85.7 ± 8.5 nm).
source: The stimulation in these animals did not increase the number of large vesicles (2.7 ± 0.6; Figure 7D). However, the diameter of these structures became 1.5 times larger (from 59.0 ± 5.9 nm to 85.7 ± 8.5 nm; Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of dynamin mutants with and without stimulation.

claim: The amount of surface area incorporated into large vesicles in stimulated dynamin mutants equals to ∼12 synaptic vesicles—the number of synaptic vesicles estimated to fuse with a single stimulus.
source: The amount of surface area incorporated into these large vesicles equals to ∼12 synaptic vesicles—the number of synaptic vesicles estimated to fuse with a single stimulus (Figure 2E,'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a calculation based on the surface area of the enlarged structures in dynamin mutants.

claim: Dynamin is required to cleave the endocytic structures from the surface.
source: These data suggest that dynamin is required to cleave the structures from the surface and that the dense projection and the adherens junctions are the endocytic sites in C. elegans neuromuscular junctions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the accumulation of structures in dynamin mutants.

claim: The dense projection and the adherens junctions are the endocytic sites in C. elegans neuromuscular junctions.
source: These data suggest that dynamin is required to cleave the structures from the surface and that the dense projection and the adherens junctions are the endocytic sites in C. elegans neuromuscular junctions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of trapped structures in dynamin mutants.

claim: Two sites observed for endocytosis at C. elegans neuromuscular junctions may correspond to the two endocytic sites observed in other organisms.
source: The two sites we observe for endocytosis, at the dense projections and adherens junctions, may correspond to the two endocytic sites observed in other organisms.
evidence: This is speculation connecting the current findings to observations in other systems.

claim: In dynamin mutants in the Drosophila retina, trapped endocytic structures are found both adjacent to the dense projection and at lateral sites.
source: For example, in dynamin mutants in the Drosophila retina, trapped endocytic structures are found both adjacent to the dense projection and at lateral sites (Koenig and Ikeda, 1996).
evidence: This is based on citation to studies in Drosophila.

claim: At the frog neuromuscular junction large indentations appear near the active zone 1 s after stimulation, in addition to small pits at lateral sites.
source: At the frog neuromuscular junction large indentations appear near the active zone 1 s after stimulation, in addition to small pits at lateral sites (Miller and Heuser, 1984).
evidence: This is based on citation to studies at the frog neuromuscular junction.

claim: Optical imaging studies were able to distinguish two sites of endocytosis.
source: Optical imaging of the frog neuromuscular junction (Richards et al., 2000; Gaffield et al., 2011), the snake neuromuscular junctions (Teng et al., 1999), and in hippocampal cultures (Vanden Berghe and Klingauf, 2006) were also able to distinguish two sites of endocytosis.
evidence: This is based on citations to optical imaging studies.

claim: These two distinctive sites may direct recycling vesicles into different pools: recycling from the active zone may be directed into the cycling pool and those from the periactive zone could be directed to the reserve pool.
source: These two distinctive sites may direct recycling vesicles into different pools: recycling from the active zone may be directed into the cycling pool and those from the periactive zone could be directed to the reserve pool (Richards et al., 2000; Vanden Berghe and Klingauf, 2006; Voglmaier and Edwards, 2007).
evidence: This is speculation about functional implications, supported by citations.
